what_it_does: Image-generation models called diffusion models work by running a large neural network dozens or hundreds of times in sequence, each pass slightly 'denoising' a blurry picture toward a sharp one. Each pass is expensive, and existing hardware treats every pass independently even though adjacent passes produce very similar numbers — the outputs barely change from one step to the next. Ditto exploits this similarity: it runs the first pass at full precision, then for every subsequent pass it computes only the tiny numerical difference from the previous pass rather than the full output. These differences are typically very small (often zero), so they can be stored and processed using fewer bits than normal — essentially using a compressed representation (fewer bits per number, also called reduced precision or lower bit-width) — and when a difference is zero, the computation is skipped entirely. The hardware accelerator is built around specialized units that efficiently handle this pattern of small, often-zero differences.
